introduction: “I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve?” The readings that follow give reasons for that question: the soul goes on, as a child goes on from the womb; it progresses without end, by grace; it keeps its individuality and its loves; those who have gone see us, and we may help them by prayer and good deeds. Much of the guide is letters to the bereaved, to a daughter, a brother, a mother who has lost a son. The oldest company is close: the vestibule of the Mishnah, Seneca’s birthday of eternity, Socrates before his judges, Paul’s spiritual body, the Qur’an’s soul at peace, and poets from Donne to Whitman. The other voices are as old. The Preacher says that the dead know nothing; Lucretius looks back before birth and sees a mirror of the nothing to come; Claudio is afraid; Swinburne is glad that no life lives for ever; the Gītā has the soul return, and the Upanishad has the river lose its name in the sea. Jesus wept at a grave.
questions: The readings compare death to birth: the child in the womb cannot imagine this world. Lucretius reasons from the time before birth to the time after death and finds nothing in either. What makes one analogy more persuasive to you than the other, and what would count as evidence for either?

Socrates thought death either a dreamless sleep or a journey, and good in both cases; the readings are sure which it is. What does certainty add to a person’s way of living, and what did Socrates manage without it?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá says that the soul returns to God as birds to a garden, not as a drop to the ocean, and that individuality remains. Set this beside the rivers of the Upanishad and the solitary coming of the Qur’an. What is each picture trying to keep?
Mothers and brothers are told not to grieve, and Jesus wept. How might a person hold the consolation of these letters together with the weeping that Paul asks us to share?

The dead may be helped by the prayers and good deeds of the living, say the readings; Abraham in the parable speaks of a gulf that cannot be crossed. What difference does it make to the way people live, and remember, which of these they believe?

The Apocalypse promises rest from labour; the readings speak of a continuation of our life and work, and of holy souls who long to return and serve. What do the two hopes say about the worth of work done here?

outside.why: “I have made death a messenger of joy to thee. Wherefore dost thou grieve?” Donne talks death down from its reputation: one short sleep past, we wake eternally, and death shall be no more.

The reading asks why one should grieve at a messenger of joy. Bacon notices where the grief comes from: men fear death as children fear the dark, and tales increase the fear. How much of what people feel about death has been taught to them?
The soul is “released from the bondage of the limited to enjoy the liberties of the unlimited”. Socrates, on his last day, describes the soul in the body as looking through the bars of a prison.

“At first it is very difficult to welcome death.” Claudio, condemned and twenty years old, says how difficult: to lie in cold obstruction and to rot; this sensible warm motion to become a kneaded clod. What does the reading ask of someone who feels that?

“The world beyond is as different from this world as this world is different from that of the child while still in the womb.” Rabbi Jacob uses a house: this world is like a vestibule before the world to come.
Bahá’u’lláh likens the life to come to birth from the womb. Seneca wrote to a friend in the same figure: that day, which you fear as being the end of all things, is the birthday of your eternity.

The soul “will continue to progress until it attaineth the presence of God”. Socrates, an hour after his sentence, allows two possibilities, a sleep without dreams or a journey to another place, and thinks either a gain. What does the reading’s certainty add to his calm?
“Death proffereth unto every confident believer the cup that is life indeed.” Paul in prison: to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.

Those who believe “enjoy that blessed life which we call life eternal”; the veiled, though alive, are as non-existent. Jesus to Martha at her brother’s grave: whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die.

“Man is immortal and everlasting.” The Preacher says flatly that the dead know not any thing, and that their love and their hatred have perished. His book stands in the same Bible as the promises. Why might a scripture keep both voices?
As the tree cannot conceive the animal or the human, “the human world has no knowledge of the Kingdom of God”. Paul: eye hath not seen, nor ear heard, the things which God hath prepared.

“Out of that world of darkness, he passed into this world of light.” Jesus uses birth for the passage his disciples dread: her hour is come; and afterwards she remembers no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born.
In the next world “all the truths of which he was ignorant before will be made plain and clear”. Paul: now I know in part; but then shall I know even as also I am known.
The reading reasons from the unborn child to the dying. Tagore reasons from the nursing child: it cries when taken from the right breast, and in the next moment finds its consolation in the left.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá looks back to the womb and argues forward to a fuller life. Lucretius looks back to the time before birth and argues forward to nothing: as that was nothing to us, so will be the time when we are gone. Which of the two readings of the past is the better mirror?
“If a human life … were limited to this earthly span, then what would be the harvest of creation?” Paul: if in this life only we have hope, we are of all men most miserable.

Without a life beyond, says the reading, the world of being “would be meaningless”. The Preacher looked at the same facts, one event to the righteous and to the wicked, and called it vanity, and still said to do one’s work. Can a life be worth living on his terms?
“We dare not, in this Day, lift the veil that concealeth the exalted station which every true believer can attain.” The Qur’an: no soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy.

“If the glass is shattered or the mirror destroyed, no harm befalls the outpouring grace of the sun.” Paul’s figure is a tent and a house: if our earthly tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God.
The spirit continues “unabated” when the body is destroyed. Krishna to Arjuna on the battlefield: never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never.

“At death everything but Spirit is destroyed and becomes extinct.” The Preacher’s last picture of dying: then shall the dust return to the earth as it was, and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá locates manliness and womanliness in the heart and not in “water and clay”. Asked whose wife a woman will be in the resurrection, Jesus answers that they neither marry nor are given in marriage, and are equal unto the angels. What of a person does each saying expect to continue?
The physical attributes “are metaphorical”; nobility belongs to the heart of either. Paul: there is neither male nor female, for ye are all one.
“All blows fall upon the earthly body and elements of dust, not upon the pure soul.” Jesus: fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul.
Paradise “in this world … is realized through love of Me and My good-pleasure”. Jesus: the kingdom of God is within you.
Those without the spirit of life “are the dead, even as Christ hath explained in the Gospel text”. This is one of the sayings meant: let the dead bury their dead.
“Ye shall shine and sparkle forevermore from the horizon of existence.” Daniel: they that be wise shall shine as the brightness of the firmament, and as the stars for ever and ever.

The “existential rewards” are perfections attained “while still abiding in this world” which are the cause of everlasting life. John gives eternal life a present tense: this is life eternal, that they might know thee.
“How often hath a sinner, at the hour of death, attained to the essence of faith.” The thief crucified beside Jesus asks to be remembered, and is answered: to day shalt thou be with me in paradise.
“And how often hath a devout believer, at the hour of his soul’s ascension, been so changed as to fall.” Paul: let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.

“In the realm of spirit there is no retreat possible, all movement is bound to be towards a perfect state.” Proverbs: the path of the just is as the shining light, that shineth more and more unto the perfect day.
After death progress is possible “through divine bestowal rather than human striving … purely through grace”. Paul says as much of this life: by grace are ye saved; it is the gift of God.

In the next world advancement “depends entirely on grace”. The Preacher draws the lesson for this one: whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might, for there is no work in the grave. Does the reading make this life matter more, or less?

“As the perfections of man are infinite, he can also advance in these perfections after his ascension.” Whitman: I am an acme of things accomplish’d, and I an encloser of things to be; I mount and mount.

There is no higher station than the human, and within it no end of perfecting. The Sermon on the Mount sets the mark that makes the work endless: be ye therefore perfect, even as your Father is perfect.
Each spirit “progresses only within that degree”: Peter’s is not Christ’s. Jesus speaks of the house itself as having room for difference: in my Father’s house are many mansions.

Righteous souls “who passed away ere they heard the Call” attained the light. The Epistle to the Hebrews honours such: these all died in faith, not having received the promises, but having seen them afar off.
“The flooding grace … of the holy Manifestations appear after Their ascension from this world.” Jesus: it is expedient for you that I go away.
The human spirit does “not return after death to this world”. The Epistle to the Hebrews: it is appointed unto men once to die.

The rational soul does not come back. The Gītā teaches that it does, as one who lays aside worn-out robes and takes new ones. Hundreds of millions have lived by each teaching. What does each make of the worth of a single life?

“A love that one may have entertained for any one will not be forgotten in the world of the Kingdom.” The Qur’an: those who believe and whose seed follow them in faith, We cause their seed to join them.
The friends “will recognize each other, and will seek union”. David, when his child has died, rises and eats: I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me.

The soul’s return to God is “not like the drop and ocean, but rather like the return of birds to the garden”. The Chāndogya Upanishad teaches the image the reading declines: rivers that become the sea and do not know, I am this or that river. What is at stake between the bird and the river?
“They observe this world and its people, for the veil has been lifted.” The Epistle to the Hebrews: we also are compassed about with so great a cloud of witnesses.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes for the soul’s waking: Now We have removed from thee thy covering, and piercing is thy sight this day.
“The state of the soul after death is like awakening from a dream.” Shelley, of Keats: he is not dead, he doth not sleep; he hath awakened from the dream of life.

In the eternal world “friendship and spiritual intimacy are naturally among the essential requisites”. The Qur’an’s gardens are entered in company, with fathers, helpmeets and children, and greeted with peace.
“When we get there this earthly existence will be to us as a dream.” Prospero: we are such stuff as dreams are made on, and our little life is rounded with a sleep.

The ties of love “will be intensified a thousand times”. The Qur’an also has a verse of great solitude: each one of them will come unto Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone. How do the readings hold the meeting with God and the company of others together?

‘Abdu’l-Bahá allows that “a conversation can be held”, of the heart and not of the mouth. Asked about serving the spirits of the dead, Confucius turned the question back: while you are not able to serve men, how can you serve their spirits? What does his refusal protect?
The Báb describes a Paradise where “every tree bears fruits of diverse hues”. The Qur’an introduces its own description with a word of caution about how to read it: a similitude of the Garden.

“The world beyond is the home of my soul, it is my America, in which you do not believe … because I cannot show it to you.” Hamlet’s name for it: the undiscover’d country from whose bourn no traveller returns.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá offers to prove the other world by taking his hearer there. Job puts the question as one who must wait for the answer: if a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come. What can be said to someone who must wait?
“Its Sun never sets … All living beings in that City are unaware of death.” John’s city: there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun.

“After the ascension of a soul, good deeds and charitable works should be performed for that soul.” Monica, dying far from home, asked one thing of her sons: that you will remember me at the Lord’s altar, wherever you be.

Good deeds done for the departed “become the cause of the elevation of its station”. In the parable Abraham tells the rich man that between them a great gulf is fixed, so that none can pass. Churches have divided over which is the truer picture. What does each ask of the living?
Believing children may “seek forgiveness and intercession” for heedless parents. Abraham in the Qur’an: our Lord! forgive me and my parents.
Those who ascended with steadfastness “witness and are aware”. The Qur’an: call not those who are slain in the way of Allah dead. Nay, they are living, only ye perceive not.
The prayer asks that a servant “may consort with Thy chosen ones … in heavenly places”. The psalm’s last line: I will dwell in the house of the Lord for ever.
“Gladden Thou their hearts in the world of the unseen.” The Qur’an’s welcome to the soul at peace: return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure; enter thou My Garden.
“The blessed souls do not wish to be established in this wilderness of a world.” Paul: willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord.
“Shall I find my mother again?” “Certainly. Separation is only in the world of bodies.” Paul to the bereaved at Thessalonica: that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope.
She “hath been delivered from all sorrow, vexation, hardship, trouble, and misfortune”. The Apocalypse: there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying.

“Grieve thou not for thy mother; for she hath been lifted up.” At the grave of a friend he was about to raise, Jesus wept. What place do these readings leave for the tears of someone who believes every word of them?

“The fruit of life was attained … However much longer she might have lived, no better result than this could have been achieved.” The Second Letter to Timothy: I have finished my course, I have kept the faith.
“That homeless bird hath winged its flight unto the sheltering nest.” Rūmī’s reed, cut from the reed-bed, laments until the day it shall return.

“The son hath not been lost but, rather, hath stepped from this world into another.” Epictetus taught his students the same refusal of the word: never say of anything, I have lost it; but, I have returned it.
A mother is asked not to wail, since her son is found. Job, told that all his children are dead, tears his robe and worships: the Lord gave, and the Lord hath taken away.

‘Abdu’l-Bahá calls the loss of a son “heart-breaking and beyond the limits of human endurance”, and asks the mother not to weep. Paul’s rule for those around her is to weep with them that weep. How do the consolation and the weeping go together at a graveside?

If that station were revealed “to an extent smaller than a needle’s eye”, people would be consumed with joy. Whitman, looking at grass on graves: to die is different from what any one supposed, and luckier.
She “found peace and tranquility”. Augustine: our hearts are restless till they rest in You.
The youth who has died is a bird of faithfulness gone to its branch. Dickinson makes death a courteous caller: he kindly stopped for me; the carriage held but just ourselves and Immortality.
“If you are grief-stricken … know that she is in the utmost joy and delight.” Isaiah: he will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces.
This is the verse ‘Abdu’l-Bahá quotes: whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily We shall quicken with good life.

“Supreme importance should be attached … not to this first creation but rather to the future life.” The phrase is the Qur’an’s: ye know the first creation; We may transfigure you and make you what ye know not.
Death is “the cause of entry into the gardens of reunion”. Tennyson, at eighty: I hope to see my Pilot face to face when I have crost the bar.

God “hath ordained death and departure from this world as one of the gates leading to the meeting with Him”. The psalm: though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.
“Two birds have winged their flight to the most exalted nest.” Hamlet, before the duel: there’s a special providence in the fall of a sparrow; the readiness is all.
“Death and life are two gates for the manifestation of divine grace.” Marcus Aurelius sets them side by side too: death is such as generation is, a mystery of nature.

The Báb parts from his companions with the promise that “joy of eternal reunion awaits us”. Swinburne gives thanks for the opposite: that no life lives for ever, that dead men rise up never. He calls it rest. What would be lost, and what spared, if he were right?
“My soul will escape like a bird at liberty from this earthly cage of my body.” Longfellow: dust thou art, to dust returnest, was not spoken of the soul.
“Praise be to God Who hath made death a door to His presence.” Job: I know that my redeemer liveth, and though worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God.

“What is death but the transference of the soul from its nether abode to its exalted habitation.” Bunyan’s Mr. Valiant-for-truth goes down into the river: so he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side.

“Through it the carpet of joy is rolled out.” FitzGerald’s Khayyám knows nothing of where he came from or where he goes: like water willy-nilly flowing, like wind along the waste. What would each say to the other across a table?
“One transformation lies ahead, and that is God’s irrevocable decree.” Paul: we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye. O death, where is thy sting?
“Death is nothing more than ascending from one world to another world more subtle than the first.” Paul: it is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body.
“Such souls exist and are not lost, are prosperous not buried, are rising not setting.” The question put to the women at the tomb: why seek ye the living among the dead?

The reading denies that the dead are lost. Macbeth, told that his wife is dead, sees only a brief candle and a tale told by an idiot. He has made himself the man who would see that. Does what a person has done with life shape what death looks like to him?
“Extinction is the essence of eternality and loss is the essence of finding.” Jesus: whosoever will lose his life for my sake shall find it.

“What they sowed in the material world they have found as a gathered harvest in the divine realm.” The Qur’an: the good deeds which endure are better in thy Lord’s sight for reward, and better in respect of hope.

Asked whether one must leave the body to return to God, or whether the true return is of the heart now, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá agrees with the second. Paul: ye are dead, and your life is hid with Christ in God.

“Immortal existence in the beyond is but a continuation of our life and work here.” The voice from heaven in the Apocalypse blesses the dead because they rest from their labours. Is heaven rest or work, and why might each have been promised?

The Holy Ones “yearn to return unto this world, and be of some service”. In the Qur’an the one who asks to be sent back is the soul that wasted its time, and a barrier stands behind it. What do the two pictures together say about the days one has now?
The prayer asks that the departed become “creators and players, singers and dancers”. The last psalm: praise him with the timbrel and dance; let every thing that hath breath praise the Lord.
A correspondent expects to settle a quarrel in the next world “by the collar”, with “fists and slaps and shouting”. The Gospel’s advice is to settle it sooner: first be reconciled to thy brother.
“We shall sit together many times again in the Kingdom … In every world of God a new Lord’s Supper is set for the faithful!” John’s vision: God himself shall be with them.

The true believer “will last as long as God, Himself, will last”. The Qur’an says that everything will perish save His countenance. How do the readings understand a creature’s lasting, if only One is everlasting in Himself?

“Sorrow not if, in these days … things contrary to your wishes have been ordained.” Paul: our light affliction, which is but for a moment, worketh for us a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory.
“Worlds, holy and spiritually glorious, will be unveiled to your eyes.” Paul: the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory which shall be revealed.
“What those worlds are and what their nature is we cannot know.” The First Epistle of John: it doth not yet appear what we shall be.

job-shall-he-live-again.text: If a man die, shall he live again? all the days of my appointed time will I wait, till my change come

job-my-redeemer-liveth.text: For I know that my redeemer liveth, and that he shall stand at the latter day upon the earth: And though after my skin worms destroy this body, yet in my flesh shall I see God: Whom I shall see for myself, and mine eyes shall behold, and not another

psalm-no-remembrance-in-death.text: For in death there is no remembrance of thee: in the grave who shall give thee thanks

psalm-death-of-his-saints.text: Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints

ecclesiastes-spirit-shall-return.text: Or ever the silver cord be loosed, or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern. Then shall the dust return to the earth as it was: and the spirit shall return unto God who gave it

ecclesiastes-dead-know-not.text: For the living know that they shall die: but the dead know not any thing, neither have they any more a reward; for the memory of them is forgotten. Also their love, and their hatred, and their envy, is now perished; neither have they any more a portion for ever in any thing that is done under the sun

isaiah-swallow-up-death.text: He will swallow up death in victory; and the Lord God will wipe away tears from off all faces; and the rebuke of his people shall he take away from off all the earth: for the Lord hath spoken it

daniel-sleep-in-the-dust.text: And many of them that sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt

samuel-i-shall-go-to-him.text: And he said, While the child was yet alive, I fasted and wept: for I said, Who can tell whether God will be gracious to me, that the child may live? But now he is dead, wherefore should I fast? can I bring him back again? I shall go to him, but he shall not return to me

john-resurrection-and-life.text: I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: And whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. Believest thou this

john-woman-in-travail.text: A woman when she is in travail hath sorrow, because her hour is come: but as soon as she is delivered of the child, she remembereth no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world. And ye now therefore have sorrow: but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and your joy no man taketh from you

luke-god-of-the-living.text: The children of this world marry, and are given in marriage: But they which shall be accounted worthy to obtain that world, and the resurrection from the dead, neither marry, nor are given in marriage: Neither can they die any more: for they are equal unto the angels; and are the children of God, being the children of the resurrection. Now that the dead are raised, even Moses shewed at the bush, when he calleth the Lord the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob. For he is not a God of the dead, but of the living: for all live unto him

luke-today-in-paradise.text: And he said unto Jesus, Lord, remember me when thou comest into thy kingdom. And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, Today shalt thou be with me in paradise

luke-great-gulf.text: And beside all this, between us and you there is a great gulf fixed: so that they which would pass from hence to you cannot; neither can they pass to us, that would come from thence

corinthians-sown-a-natural-body.text: So also is the resurrection of the dead. It is sown in corruption; it is raised in incorruption: It is sown in dishonour; it is raised in glory: it is sown in weakness; it is raised in power: It is sown a natural body; it is raised a spiritual body. There is a natural body, and there is a spiritual body

corinthians-death-where-is-thy-sting.text: Behold, I shew you a mystery; We shall not all sleep, but we shall all be changed, In a moment, in the twinkling of an eye, at the last trump: for the trumpet shall sound, and the dead shall be raised incorruptible, and we shall be changed. For this corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal must put on immortality. So when this corruptible shall have put on incorruption, and this mortal shall have put on immortality, then shall be brought to pass the saying that is written, Death is swallowed up in victory. O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory

corinthians-in-this-life-only.text: If in this life only we have hope in Christ, we are of all men most miserable

corinthians-eat-and-drink.text: If after the manner of men I have fought with beasts at Ephesus, what advantageth it me, if the dead rise not? let us eat and drink; for to morrow we die

corinthians-earthly-house.text: For we know that if our earthly house of this tabernacle were dissolved, we have a building of God, an house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens

corinthians-absent-from-the-body.text: Therefore we are always confident, knowing that, whilst we are at home in the body, we are absent from the Lord: (For we walk by faith, not by sight:) We are confident, I say, and willing rather to be absent from the body, and to be present with the Lord

thessalonians-sorrow-not.text: But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. For if we believe that Jesus died and rose again, even so them also which sleep in Jesus will God bring with him

hebrews-once-to-die.text: And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment

revelation-rest-from-their-labours.text: And I heard a voice from heaven saying unto me, Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them

revelation-no-night-there.text: And there shall be no more curse: but the throne of God and of the Lamb shall be in it; and his servants shall serve him: And they shall see his face; and his name shall be in their foreheads. And there shall be no night there; and they need no candle, neither light of the sun; for the Lord God giveth them light: and they shall reign for ever and ever

quran-call-them-not-dead.text: And call not those who are slain in the way of Allah "dead." Nay, they are living, only ye perceive not.

quran-kept-hid-of-joy.text: No soul knoweth what is kept hid for them of joy, as a reward for what they used to do.

quran-receiveth-souls-in-sleep.text: Allah receiveth (men's) souls at the time of their death, and that (soul) which dieth not (yet) in its sleep. He keepeth that (soul) for which He hath ordained death and dismisseth the rest till an appointed term. Lo! herein verily are portents for people who take thought.

quran-good-life.text: Whosoever doeth right, whether male or female, and is a believer, him verily we shall quicken with good life, and We shall pay them a recompense in proportion to the best of what they used to do.

quran-families-join-them.text: And they who believe and whose seed follow them in faith, We cause their seed to join them (there), and We deprive them of nought of their (life's) work. Every man is a pledge for that which he hath earned.

quran-come-solitary.text: Now have ye come unto Us solitary as We did create you at the first, and ye have left behind you all that We bestowed upon you, and We behold not with you those your intercessors, of whom ye claimed that they possessed a share in you. Now is the bond between you severed, and that which ye presumed hath failed you.

quran-come-alone.text: And each one of them will come unto Him on the Day of Resurrection, alone.

quran-soul-at-peace.text: But ah! thou soul at peace! Return unto thy Lord, content in His good pleasure! Enter thou among My bondmen! Enter thou My Garden

quran-send-me-back.text: Until, when death cometh unto one of them, he saith: My Lord! Send me back, That I may do right in that which I have left behind! But nay! It is but a word that he speaketh; and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised

quran-what-ye-know-not.text: We mete out death among you, and We are not to be outrun, That We may transfigure you and make you what ye know not. And verily ye know the first creation. Why, then, do ye not reflect

quran-gardens-of-eden-with-their-fathers.text: Gardens of Eden which they enter, along with all who do right of their fathers and their helpmeets and their seed. The angels enter unto them from every gate, (Saying): Peace be unto you because ye persevered. Ah, passing sweet will be the sequel of the (heavenly) Home

plato-death-one-of-two-things.text: there is great reason to hope that death is a good, for one of two things: - either death is a state of nothingness and utter unconsciousness, or, as men say, there is a change and migration of the soul from this world to another
plato-death-one-of-two-things.author: Plato

marcus-mystery-of-nature.text: Death is such as generation is, a mystery of nature
marcus-mystery-of-nature.author: Marcus Aurelius

seneca-birthday-of-eternity.text: That day, which you fear as being the end of all things, is the birthday of your eternity
seneca-birthday-of-eternity.author: Seneca

rights.note: Published in the United States in 1925; translator d. 1969. One sentence.

lucretius-nothing-to-us.text: Look back: / Nothing to us was all fore-passed eld / Of time the eternal, ere we had a birth. / And Nature holds this like a mirror up / Of time-to-be when we are dead and gone
lucretius-nothing-to-us.author: Lucretius

augustine-remember-me-at-the-altar.text: Lay this body anywhere, let not the care for it trouble you at all. This only I ask, that you will remember me at the Lord's altar, wherever you be
augustine-remember-me-at-the-altar.author: Augustine of Hippo
augustine-remember-me-at-the-altar.locator: IX.11 (the words of his mother Monica)

bacon-fear-to-go-in-the-dark.text: Men fear Death, as children fear to go in the dark; and as that natural fear in children is increased with tales, so is the other
bacon-fear-to-go-in-the-dark.author: Francis Bacon

gita-never-the-spirit-was-born.text: Never the spirit was born; the spirit shall cease to be never; / Never was time it was not; End and Beginning are dreams!

whitman-luckier.text: They are alive and well somewhere, / The smallest sprout shows there is really no death, / And if ever there was it led forward life, and does not wait at the end to arrest it, / And ceas'd the moment life appear'd. / All goes onward and outward, nothing collapses, / And to die is different from what any one supposed, and luckier
whitman-luckier.author: Walt Whitman

tagore-left-breast.text: And because I love this life, I know I shall love death as well. The child cries out when from the right breast the mother takes it away, in the very next moment to find in the left one its consolation
tagore-left-breast.author: Rabindranath Tagore

shakespeare-go-we-know-not-where.text: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; / To lie in cold obstruction and to rot; / This sensible warm motion to become / A kneaded clod
shakespeare-go-we-know-not-where.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shakespeare-readiness-is-all.text: there's a special providence in the fall of a sparrow. If it be now, 'tis not to come; if it be not to come, it will be now; if it be not now, yet it will come: the readiness is all
shakespeare-readiness-is-all.author: William Shakespeare

source.label: The Complete Works of William Shakespeare (MIT)

shelley-dream-of-life.text: Peace, peace! he is not dead, he doth not sleep— / He hath awakened from the dream of life
shelley-dream-of-life.author: Percy Bysshe Shelley

bunyan-trumpets-sounded.text: When the day that he must go hence was come, many accompanied him to the river-side, into which as he went he said, "Death, where is thy sting?" And, as he went down deeper, he said, "Grave, where is thy victory?" So he passed over, and all the trumpets sounded for him on the other side
bunyan-trumpets-sounded.author: John Bunyan
bunyan-trumpets-sounded.locator: Part II, the passing of Mr. Valiant-for-truth

longfellow-not-spoken-of-the-soul.text: Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal; / Dust thou art, to dust returnest, / Was not spoken of the soul
longfellow-not-spoken-of-the-soul.author: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow

swinburne-weariest-river.text: From too much love of living, / From hope and fear set free, / We thank with brief thanksgiving / Whatever gods may be / That no life lives for ever; / That dead men rise up never; / That even the weariest river / Winds somewhere safe to sea
swinburne-weariest-river.author: Algernon Charles Swinburne

dickinson-could-not-stop-for-death.text: Because I could not stop for Death, / He kindly stopped for me; / The carriage held but just ourselves / And Immortality
dickinson-could-not-stop-for-death.author: Emily Dickinson
dickinson-could-not-stop-for-death.work: “Because I could not stop for Death”

tennyson-crossing-the-bar.text: For tho' from out our bourne of Time and Place / The flood may bear me far, / I hope to see my Pilot face to face / When I have crost the bar
tennyson-crossing-the-bar.author: Alfred Tennyson
